title: Data Modeling and Management
summary: Choose the right objects, relationships and field types, and move data in, out or keep it outside with Salesforce Connect.

lessons.title: Objects, fields and Schema Builder
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate data model.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Salesforce keeps data in **objects**. An object is a table for one kind of thing, like accounts or invoices. Each **record** is one row in it. Each **field** is one column, like a name or a date. Your **data model** is the set of objects and the links between them.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A filing cabinet. Each drawer is an object. Each folder in a drawer is a record. Each line on the form inside is a field. Where it stops: Salesforce folders can point at folders in other drawers. Those links are relationships.

cards.title: Kinds of objects
items: **Standard objects** come with Salesforce: Account, Contact, Opportunity, Case.
**Custom objects** are ones you build. Their API names end in `__c`.
**External objects** show data that lives outside Salesforce. Their API names end in `__x`.
Platform events and big objects are special kinds for messages and huge archives.

cards.title: Reuse first
cards.body: Before you build, check the **standard objects**. If Case already fits support tickets, use Case and add fields. Build a **custom object** only when nothing standard fits what you track. Standard objects come with ready features, like lead conversion or case queues.

cards.title: Schema Builder
cards.body: **Schema Builder** draws your objects and their links as a diagram. You can also create objects and fields right there, including relationship and formula fields. Dragging a box around the canvas only moves the picture. It never changes the data model.

cards.title: How many fields fit?
cards.body: Each object has a **custom field limit** set by the edition. Professional allows 100, Enterprise 500, Unlimited and Performance 800, Developer 500. A **geolocation** field counts as 3 fields. A custom address field counts as 9.

Moving objects around in Schema Builder doesn't rearrange page layouts or change relationships. It's only the view. Also, don't build a custom object for something a standard object already does well.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Object = drawer. Record = folder. Field = line on the form. Schema Builder = the map on the wall.

terms.say: Tables that hold one kind of thing, like accounts or invoices.
One row in an object. One account, one invoice, one person.
One column in an object, like Name or Close Date. Every record has a spot for it.
The plan of all your objects and how they connect to each other.
Objects that come with Salesforce, like Account and Contact. You can add fields to them.
An object you build yourself for something Salesforce doesn't track yet. Its API name ends in __c.
Objects that show data still stored in another system. Salesforce reads it, it doesn't keep a copy.
A Setup tool that draws your objects and their links as a picture. You can add objects and fields there too.
The most custom fields one object can have. It depends on your Salesforce edition.
A field that stores a spot on the map as latitude and longitude. It counts as 3 fields.

lessons.title: Lookup or master-detail?
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, explain the capabilities of the various relationship types and the implications of each on record access, user interface, and reporting.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **relationship field** links a record to a parent record. There are two main kinds. A **lookup** is a loose link: the child can live on its own. A **master-detail** is a tight link: the child (the **detail**) can't exist without its parent (the **master**).

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A lookup is a sticky note saying "see this file". Remove the file and the note just goes blank. Master-detail is a page stapled into a binder. Throw away the binder and its pages go too. Where it stops: you can choose other lookup delete options too.

cards.title: Master-detail rules
items: Delete the master and its details are deleted. Undelete it and they come back.
Details have **no Owner field**. The master's owner owns them.
Details get the master's sharing and security.
The master field is **required** on the detail.
Reparenting is off unless you tick **Allow reparenting**.

cards.title: Lookup rules
items: Can be optional or required.
If optional and the parent is deleted: **Clear the value** (default), **Don't allow deletion**, or **Delete this record also**.
Delete this record also is a **cascade delete**. It's off by default, Salesforce must turn it on, and it skips security.
A link from an object to itself must be a lookup.

cards.title: Limits
cards.body: Each custom object can have **2 master-detail** fields and **40 relationships** in total. Standard objects can't be the detail of a custom object. You can't add a master-detail field to an object that **already has data**. Build a lookup, fill it on every record, then convert it.

Picking lookup when the child must vanish with its parent, or must share its parent's security. Only master-detail gives both built in. And a third parent link? It must be a lookup: the master-detail limit is 2.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Lookup = sticky note: loose, own owner. Master-detail = staple: tight, shared fate, shared owner.

terms.say: A field that points to another record, so the two are linked.
A loose link to another record. The child keeps its own owner and lives on its own.
A tight link. The child belongs to its parent, shares its owner and security, and is deleted with it.
The child side of a master-detail link. It can't exist without its master.
The parent side of a master-detail link. It controls its details.
Detail records don't have their own owner. Whoever owns the master owns them too.
A setting that lets you move a detail record to a different master. It's off by default.
Deleting a parent also deletes its children. For lookups it's off until Salesforce turns it on.
The default lookup choice. If the parent is deleted, the child's link just goes blank.
An object with records in it. You can't add a master-detail field straight away; use a lookup first.

lessons.title: Many-to-many: junction objects
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate data model.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes both sides have many. A student takes many courses, and a course has many students. Salesforce models this **many-to-many** link with a **junction object**: a custom object in the middle with **two master-detail fields**, one to each side.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A class sign-up sheet. Each line pairs one student with one course. The sheet is the junction object. Each line is a junction record. Where it stops: a junction record can also hold its own fields, like a grade or a sign-up date.

cards.title: A junction object
cards.code:
Enrollment__c (junction)
  Course__c   master-detail -> Course__c   (created first: primary)
  Student__c  master-detail -> Student__c  (created second: secondary)
  Grade__c    picklist
cards.body: One enrollment record links one student to one course.

cards.title: Junction rules
items: The **first** master-detail you create is the **primary**. It sets the look, like color and icon.
Delete the primary field, and the **secondary** becomes primary.
Delete either master, and its junction records are deleted.
Seeing a junction record needs access to **both masters**.
Roll-up summaries can go on both masters.

cards.title: Limits
cards.body: A junction object can't be the master of another master-detail. Both masters can't be the same object. And you can't delete a parent with more than **200** junction records if the junction rolls up to the other parent.
Two lookups on the middle object is not the same thing. Lookups give no roll-up summaries, no shared delete and no inherited sharing. The exam's junction object uses two master-detail fields.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Many-to-many? Put a junction in the middle, with two masters. First one created leads.

terms.say: When one record on each side can link to many on the other. Many students, many courses.
A middle object that links two others. Each of its records pairs one record from each side.
The two tight links a junction object needs, one to each parent object.
The first master-detail on a junction. It decides the junction's look, like its color and icon.
The second master-detail on a junction. It becomes primary if the first one is deleted.
To see a junction record, you need access to the parent records on both sides.
Fields on a parent that count or add up its children, like the number of enrollments.
Over 200 junction records plus a roll-up to the other parent? Then you can't delete that parent until there are fewer.

lessons.title: Hierarchical, external and indirect lookups
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, explain the capabilities of the various relationship types and the implications of each on record access, user interface, and reporting.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Besides lookup and master-detail, Salesforce has three special links. A **hierarchical** relationship links one user to another user. An **external lookup** and an **indirect lookup** link to or from **external objects**: data that stays in another system.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Hierarchical is an org chart: each person points to their boss. External links are like a library card that points to a book in another library. Where it stops: the other library has to agree on which number identifies each book.

cards.title: Hierarchical
cards.body: A **hierarchical** relationship exists **only on the User object**. A common example is a Manager field that points to another user. A user can't point to themselves, directly or through others.

cards.title: External and indirect lookups
items: **External lookup**: the child is any object; the parent is an **external object**. It matches on the parent's **External ID**.
**Indirect lookup**: the child is an **external object**; the parent is a standard or custom object. It matches on a custom field marked **unique** and **External ID**.

cards.title: Pick the link
cards.code:
Child: Order__x (external)  -> Parent: Account (in Salesforce)
   = indirect lookup, matched on Account.Customer_Number__c

Child: Case (in Salesforce) -> Parent: Shipment__x (external)
   = external lookup, matched on Shipment__x External ID
cards.body: The direction decides the type. Ask: where is the parent?

Indirect and external sound alike. Check the parent. Parent outside Salesforce: external lookup. Parent inside Salesforce, child outside: indirect lookup. And external objects can't use master-detail at all.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: External lookup: looking OUT to an external parent. Indirect lookup: an outside child finding its way IN, by a unique external ID.

terms.say: A special link from one user to another user, like an employee to their manager.
Hierarchical links can be built on users and nothing else.
A link from any record to a parent that lives outside Salesforce, as an external object.
A link from an outside record to a parent inside Salesforce, matched on a unique ID field.
Objects that show data still kept in another system. Their API names end in __x.
A field that holds the record's ID from another system, so records can be matched up.
No two records may have the same value in this field.

lessons.title: What a relationship changes
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, explain the capabilities of the various relationship types and the implications of each on record access, user interface, and reporting.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Your relationship choice changes three things. **Record access**: who can see the child. **The UI**: required fields and related lists. **Reporting**: which records show up together in a report.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Choosing between a roommate and a guest. A guest (lookup) keeps their own key. A roommate on the lease (master-detail) shares the house key and the rules. Where it stops: an admin can still give a guest extra keys with sharing.

cards.title: Access
items: Master-detail: the detail **inherits** the master's sharing. Its org-wide default is **Controlled by Parent**.
Lookup: the child keeps its own owner and its own sharing settings.

cards.title: UI and reports
items: Both kinds can add a **related list** to the parent's page layout.
Master-detail makes the field required on the detail.
A **custom report type** can follow the relationship, like "Projects with Tasks".
Master-detail allows **roll-up summary** fields on the master.

cards.title: Converting
cards.body: **Master-detail to lookup** sets the child's org-wide default to Public Read/Write. It's blocked while the master has roll-up summary fields. **Lookup to master-detail** needs a value in every record, and sets the default to Controlled by Parent.
After converting master-detail to lookup, the child is suddenly Public Read/Write. Check its sharing before users notice. And delete the roll-up summaries first, or the conversion is blocked.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: A relationship decides three things: who sees, what shows, what reports. Access, UI, reports.

terms.say: Who is allowed to see or edit a record.
Gets its settings from the parent, instead of having its own.
A sharing default for details: if you can see the master, you get that access to its details.
The baseline access everyone has to records of an object they don't own.
A list on a record's page that shows its linked child records.
A recipe that tells reports which objects to show together, following their links.
A field on a master that counts or adds up its detail records.
Everyone can see and edit every record of that object.

lessons.title: Picking field types and picklists
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the considerations when selecting or changing a field data type.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Every field has a **data type**. It decides what can go in: text, a number, a date, a yes/no checkbox, a choice from a list. The right type keeps data clean, makes reports easy and lets formulas work.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Boxes on a paper form. A box with tick marks only takes yes or no. A date box only takes a date. A list of options keeps spellings the same. Where it stops: Salesforce checks the type for you on every save.

cards.title: Picklist choices
items: **Restricted picklist**: only listed values save, even through the API.
**Global value set**: one list of values shared by many picklist fields. It's always restricted.
**Dependent picklist**: its choices are filtered by a controlling picklist or checkbox.
**Multi-select picklist**: many values at once. Harder to report and filter on.

cards.title: Text sizes
cards.body: A Text field holds up to 255 characters. A **long text area** holds 32,768 by default, and you can set 256 to 131,072. Each object holds 1,638,400 characters across its long and rich text fields. An **auto number** gives each record a unique number, up to 30 characters.

cards.title: Record types
cards.body: A **record type** can show a subset of a picklist's values to different users. All values live in the **master picklist**. Each record type picks the values it offers.
Reaching for a multi-select picklist when one value per record would do. It's harder to filter, report and change later. In reports and formulas you need `includes` instead of a plain equals.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Pick the narrowest box that fits the data. Clean in, clean out.

terms.say: What kind of value a field holds: text, number, date, checkbox and so on.
A pick list that refuses any value an admin didn't add, even from imports or the API.
One shared list of choices that many picklist fields can use.
A pick list whose choices change based on what you picked in another field.
A pick list where you can choose more than one value at once.
A big text box for long notes, up to 131,072 characters.
A field that gives each new record the next number by itself, like INV-0042.
A way to give different users different picklist values, page layouts and processes for one object.
The full list of a picklist's values. Each record type shows only some of them.

lessons.title: Changing a field's type safely
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the considerations when selecting or changing a field data type.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: You can change a custom field's type after it holds data. But some changes **lose data**, and some aren't allowed at all. Check the list first, and back up the data before you change it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Pouring water from a jug into a smaller cup. Some pours fit fine, some spill. Where it stops: Salesforce doesn't warn about every record that will spill. Plan before you pour.

cards.title: Changes that can lose data
items: To or from Date or Date/Time
To Number, Percent or Currency, from any type
From Checkbox, or from a multi-select picklist
To a multi-select picklist: values not in the list are dropped
From Auto Number, or to Auto Number from anything but Text
Text to Picklist; Long Text Area to most types

cards.title: Not allowed
items: Changing **to or from a formula** field
Changing a field mapped for **lead conversion**
Changing a field used by Apex, Visualforce, processes or flows
Changing an encrypted field

cards.title: Safe moves
cards.body: **Picklist to checkbox** lets you map which values become checked. Picklist to multi-select keeps the value. Text to Auto Number keeps the data. An External ID stays one only as Text, Number or Email.
If data is lost, list views that use the field are deleted. And you can't "just switch" a number field into a formula. Make a new formula field instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Formula fields never convert. Dates, numbers and checkboxes spill. Back up first.

terms.say: Some values get cut or wiped when the field changes type.
A formula field can't become another type, and no field can become a formula.
Turning a lead into an account, contact and opportunity. Fields mapped for it can't change type.
A safe change. You choose which picklist values become a checked box.
A field holding a record's ID from another system. It only stays one as Text, Number or Email.
Saved filtered lists of records, like "My open cases".
Save a copy of the data first, so you can bring it back if something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Importing and exporting data
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the options and considerations when importing and exporting data, including the capabilities of external data sources.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Importing means loading records into Salesforce from a file. Exporting means getting them out. The two main tools are the **Data Import Wizard**, which runs in your browser, and **Data Loader**, an app you install.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: The Data Import Wizard is a shopping basket: easy, but it only holds so much. Data Loader is a delivery truck: more setup, carries far more, and drives both ways. Where it stops: the basket also can't carry some items at all.

cards.title: Data Import Wizard
items: Up to **50,000** records at a time
Accounts, contacts, leads, solutions, campaign members and custom objects
**Can't** import opportunities, cases, campaigns, contracts, assets, documents or products
Import only: **no export**
Can match to prevent duplicates, and choose whether to fire workflow rules and processes

cards.title: Data Loader
items: Up to **5 million** records
Insert, update, **upsert**, delete and **export**
Works with standard and custom objects, including opportunities
Has a command line for scheduled jobs (Windows only)

cards.title: Backups and duplicates
cards.body: The **Data Export Service** in Setup makes backup files of your data, weekly or monthly. **Matching rules** decide what counts as a duplicate. **Duplicate rules** decide what happens: warn the user or block the save. Clean the file before you import.
Picking the Data Import Wizard for opportunities or for 200,000 records. It can't do either. That's a Data Loader job. Also, the wizard can't export.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Wizard: small, simple, in. Loader: big, any object, in and out.

terms.say: A simple import tool inside Salesforce. It loads up to 50,000 records of common objects.
An app you install to load, change, delete or export up to 5 million records.
Update the record if it already exists, insert it if it doesn't. Matching uses an ID or External ID.
The import wizard only brings data in. It can't take data out.
A Setup tool that packs your data into backup files, weekly or monthly.
Rules that decide when two records count as the same person or company.
Rules that decide what happens with a duplicate: warn the user or block the save.
Copy records out of Salesforce into a file, like a CSV.

lessons.title: External data with Salesforce Connect
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the options and considerations when importing and exporting data, including the capabilities of external data sources.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes data should stay where it is, in another system. **Salesforce Connect** shows that data inside Salesforce as **external objects**. It reads the data **in real time**, without copying it in.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A window into the shop next door. You see their shelves live, but the goods stay in their shop. Where it stops: if their shop is closed (the system is down), you see nothing.

cards.title: When to use it
items: Lots of data you don't want to store in Salesforce
Users need only a few records at a time
Users need the latest values, in real time

cards.title: What works
cards.body: External objects work with global search, lookups, record feeds, the mobile app, Apex, SOQL, change sets and packages. They're **read-only by default**. They can be writable if the data source allows it. Salesforce Connect is included in Developer Edition and costs extra in Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited.

cards.title: External Services
cards.body: Need to call another system's actions, not show its tables? **External Services** reads an **OpenAPI** description of a REST service. It turns each operation into an action you can use in Flow, with no code.

Picking a nightly import when users need the latest values and storage is tight. Salesforce Connect is the no-copy, real-time answer. And external objects only use lookup, external lookup and indirect lookup links. No master-detail.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Connect = look, don't copy. External Services = call, don't code.

terms.say: A feature that shows data from another system inside Salesforce, live, without copying it.
Objects that show outside data. The records stay in the other system.
Right now, the latest values, fetched when you look.
At first you can only look. Editing works only if the data source is set up to allow it.
A tool that turns another system's web actions into Flow actions, with no code.
A standard file that describes what a web service can do and what it needs.
The search bar at the top of Salesforce that looks across many objects at once.

flashcards.front: What is an object, a record and a field?
flashcards.back: An **object** is a table for one kind of thing. A **record** is one row in it. A **field** is one column, like Name.

flashcards.front: What does dragging objects around in Schema Builder change?
flashcards.back: Nothing in the org. It only moves the diagram. Creating objects or fields there does save to the org.

flashcards.front: How many custom fields can one object have?
flashcards.back: Professional 100, Enterprise 500, Unlimited and Performance 800, Developer 500. A geolocation field counts as 3; a custom address field counts as 9.

flashcards.front: What happens to detail records when the master is deleted?
flashcards.back: They're deleted too. Undelete the master and they come back.

flashcards.front: Who owns a detail record in master-detail?
flashcards.back: The master's owner. Details have **no Owner field**, so no sharing rules, manual sharing or queues.

flashcards.front: How many master-detail relationships can a custom object have?
flashcards.back: **2** master-detail, and **40** relationships in total.

flashcards.front: How do you add master-detail to an object that already has data?
flashcards.back: Create a lookup, fill it on every record, then convert it to master-detail.

flashcards.front: How do you model a many-to-many relationship?
flashcards.back: A **junction object** with **two master-detail** fields, one to each side.

flashcards.front: Which master-detail on a junction is the primary?
flashcards.back: The **first** one created. It sets the junction's look and feel. Delete it, and the secondary becomes primary.

flashcards.front: What access does a user need to see a junction record?
flashcards.back: Access to **both** master records.

flashcards.front: Where can you create a hierarchical relationship?
flashcards.back: Only on the **User** object. Example: a Manager field pointing to another user.

flashcards.front: External lookup or indirect lookup: what's the difference?
flashcards.back: **External lookup**: parent is an external object, matched on its External ID. **Indirect lookup**: child is external, parent is in Salesforce, matched on a unique, External ID field.

flashcards.front: Can an external object use master-detail?
flashcards.back: No. External objects only use lookup, external lookup and indirect lookup.

flashcards.front: What happens to sharing when you convert master-detail to lookup?
flashcards.back: The child's org-wide default becomes **Public Read/Write**. It's blocked while the master has roll-up summary fields.

flashcards.front: What happens when you convert a lookup to master-detail?
flashcards.back: Every record needs a value first. The child's org-wide default becomes **Controlled by Parent**.

flashcards.front: How does a relationship affect reports?
flashcards.back: Custom report types follow relationships, so you can report on a parent with its children.

flashcards.front: What does a restricted picklist do?
flashcards.back: It only accepts values the admin defined, even through the API.

flashcards.front: What is a global value set?
flashcards.back: One shared list of picklist values that many fields can use. It's always restricted.

flashcards.front: How big can a long text area be?
flashcards.back: Up to **131,072** characters. The default is 32,768, and the smallest is 256.

flashcards.front: How do record types use picklists?
flashcards.back: Each record type offers a subset of the values in the **master picklist**.

flashcards.front: Can you convert a field to or from a formula?
flashcards.back: No. Formula fields can't be converted, and no field can become one. Create a new formula field instead.

flashcards.front: Which field type changes can lose data?
flashcards.back: To or from Date; to Number, Percent or Currency; from Checkbox; to or from multi-select; Text to Picklist; most Auto Number and long text changes.

flashcards.front: When is changing a field's type not allowed?
flashcards.back: When it's mapped for lead conversion, used by Apex, Visualforce, processes or flows, encrypted, or to or from a formula.

flashcards.front: Data Import Wizard or Data Loader?
flashcards.back: Wizard: in the browser, up to 50,000 records, common objects, no export. Data Loader: installed app, up to 5 million, any object, with export.

flashcards.front: What can't the Data Import Wizard import?
flashcards.back: Opportunities, cases, campaigns, contracts, assets, documents and products.

flashcards.front: What does upsert do?
flashcards.back: Updates records that match, and inserts the rest. It matches on a record ID or an External ID field.

flashcards.front: How do you back up all your data on a schedule?
flashcards.back: Use the **Data Export Service** in Setup. It makes backup files weekly or monthly.

flashcards.front: What does Salesforce Connect do?
flashcards.back: Shows data from another system as **external objects**, live, without copying it into Salesforce.

flashcards.front: Can users edit external object records?
flashcards.back: Not by default: they're read-only. They can be writable if the data source allows it.

flashcards.front: What are External Services for?
flashcards.back: They turn a REST API's OpenAPI description into actions you can use in Flow, with no code.

The relationships between the moved objects are rebuilt to match
The fields on each object's page layout are reordered
The order of the object tabs in the app changes
